notes.line: d4 c6 c4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 a6 g3 Bg4
notes.teaches: Against a fianchetto setup the long diagonal is the opponent's best asset, so trade or tie down the pieces that make it work. Pinning the knight that supports the centre does both jobs at once: it slows the break they need and it offers a trade they must decide about before castling.
notes.explains: The bishop comes out to g4 onto the knight on f3, which is the piece holding the centre together while the other bishop takes the long diagonal.

notes.line: d4 c6 c4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 a6 g3 Bg4 Ne5 Bh5
notes.teaches: When a knight jumps forward to break a pin, stepping back along the same diagonal is usually better than taking. Capturing hands them a developed piece and a repaired structure; retreating keeps the tension, and the knight that jumped has to justify a square it cannot hold.
notes.explains: The bishop slides to h5, staying on the diagonal and now leaning on the pawn on e2. Nothing has been traded, and the advanced knight still has to be defended or moved again.
